claim: Neurostimulation of the hippocampal formation has shown promising results for modulating memory.
source: Neurostimulation of the hippocampal formation has shown promising results for modulating memory but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: The effects of neurostimulation on hippocampal theta-nested gamma oscillations are unknown.
source: In particular, the effects on hippocampal theta-nested gamma oscillations and theta phase reset, which are both crucial for memory processes, are unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Theta-nested gamma oscillations are crucial for memory processes.
source: In particular, the effects on hippocampal theta-nested gamma oscillations and theta phase reset, which are both crucial for memory processes, are unknown.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the introduction section.

claim: Theta phase reset is crucial for memory processes.
source: In particular, the effects on hippocampal theta-nested gamma oscillations and theta phase reset, which are both crucial for memory processes, are unknown.
evidence: This is supported by citations in the introduction section.

claim: Current computational models cannot investigate the effects of neurostimulation on theta-nested gamma oscillations and theta phase reset because they consider theta oscillations with fixed amplitude and phase velocity.
source: Moreover, these effects cannot be investigated using current computational models, which consider theta oscillations with a fixed amplitude and phase velocity.
evidence: This is a limitation identified by the authors based on their review of existing models.

claim: The authors developed a novel computational model that includes the medial septum represented as Kuramoto oscillators producing a dynamical theta rhythm with phase reset.
source: Here, we developed a novel computational model that includes the medial septum, represented as a set of abstract Kuramoto oscillators producing a dynamical theta rhythm with phase reset, and the hippocampal formation, composed of biophysically realistic neurons and able to generate theta-nested gamma oscillations under theta drive.
evidence: This describes the main methodological contribution of the paper.

claim: The hippocampal formation in the model is composed of biophysically realistic neurons and able to generate theta-nested gamma oscillations under theta drive.
source: Here, we developed a novel computational model that includes the medial septum, represented as a set of abstract Kuramoto oscillators producing a dynamical theta rhythm with phase reset, and the hippocampal formation, composed of biophysically realistic neurons and able to generate theta-nested gamma oscillations under theta drive.
evidence: This describes the hippocampal component of the model.

claim: For theta inputs just below the threshold to induce self-sustained theta-nested gamma oscillations, a single stimulation pulse can switch the network behavior from non-oscillatory to a state producing sustained oscillations.
source: We showed that, for theta inputs just below the threshold to induce self-sustained theta-nested gamma oscillations, a single stimulation pulse could switch the network behavior from non-oscillatory to a state producing sustained oscillations.
evidence: This is a key finding from the simulations presented in the results section.

claim: For a weaker theta input, pulse train stimulation at the theta frequency can transiently restore seemingly physiological oscillations.
source: Next, we demonstrated that, for a weaker theta input, pulse train stimulation at the theta frequency could transiently restore seemingly physiological oscillations.
evidence: This is another key finding from the simulations.

claim: The presence of phase reset influences whether the effects of stimulation depend on the phase at which stimulation onset is delivered.
source: Importantly, the presence of phase reset influenced whether these two effects depended on the phase at which stimulation onset was delivered, which has practical implications for designing neurostimulation protocols that are triggered by the phase of ongoing theta oscillations.
evidence: This is a key finding regarding the role of phase reset in determining phase-dependent effects.

claim: Deep brain stimulation of the entorhinal area or hippocampus has been shown to enhance memory encoding.
source: In the context of learning and memory, deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the entorhinal area or hippocampus has been shown to either enhance (Suthana et al., 2012; Suthana and Fried, 2014; Titiz et al., 2017; Jun et al., 2019) or disrupt (Jacobs et al., 2016; Goyal et al., 2018; Lozano et al., 2016) memory encoding.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: Deep brain stimulation of the entorhinal area or hippocampus has been shown to disrupt memory encoding.
source: In the context of learning and memory, deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the entorhinal area or hippocampus has been shown to either enhance (Suthana et al., 2012; Suthana and Fried, 2014; Titiz et al., 2017; Jun et al., 2019) or disrupt (Jacobs et al., 2016; Goyal et al., 2018; Lozano et al., 2016) memory encoding.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: Conflicting results regarding memory outcomes from DBS may originate from differences in experimental protocols and poor understanding of biophysical underpinnings.
source: These conflicting results may originate from differences in experimental protocols and from a poor understanding of their biophysical underpinnings.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of conflicting experimental results.

claim: The involvement of hippocampal theta oscillations and their interactions with gamma oscillations in memory-related processes has been reported in multiple studies.
source: Among such mechanisms, the involvement of hippocampal theta oscillations (4–12 Hz) and their interactions with higher-frequency gamma oscillations (30–120 Hz) in memory-related processes has been reported in multiple studies (Lisman et al., 2005; de Almeida et al., 2007; Lega et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2017; Malkov et al., 2022; Abbaspoor et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by the cited studies.

claim: Hippocampal theta oscillations occur in the 4–12 Hz frequency range.
source: Among such mechanisms, the involvement of hippocampal theta oscillations (4–12 Hz) and their interactions with higher-frequency gamma oscillations (30–120 Hz) in memory-related processes has been reported in multiple studies (Lisman et al., 2005; de Almeida et al., 2007; Lega et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2017; Malkov et al., 2022; Abbaspoor et al., 2023).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the frequency range of theta oscillations.

claim: Gamma oscillations occur in the 30–120 Hz frequency range.
source: Among such mechanisms, the involvement of hippocampal theta oscillations (4–12 Hz) and their interactions with higher-frequency gamma oscillations (30–120 Hz) in memory-related processes has been reported in multiple studies (Lisman et al., 2005; de Almeida et al., 2007; Lega et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2017; Malkov et al., 2022; Abbaspoor et al., 2023).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the frequency range of gamma oscillations.

claim: Theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling correlates with the efficacy of memory encoding and retrieval.
source: Moreover, the modulation of gamma oscillations by the phase of theta oscillations in hippocampal circuits, a phenomenon termed theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling (PAC), correlates with the efficacy of memory encoding and retrieval (Jensen and Colgin, 2007; Tort et al., 2009; Canolty and Knight, 2010; Axmacher et al., 2010; Fell and Axmacher, 2011; Lisman and Jensen, 2013; Lega et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited studies.

claim: Coupling between oscillatory rhythms originates from different neural architectures and correlates with a range of behavioral and cognitive functions.
source: Experimental and computational work on the coupling between oscillatory rhythms has indicated that it originates from different neural architectures and correlates with a range of behavioral and cognitive functions, enabling the long-range synchronization of cortical areas and facilitating multi-item encoding in the context of memory (Hyafil et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited work.

claim: Theta burst stimulation optimally induces long-term potentiation.
source: Neurostimulation protocols that affect these rhythms, such as theta burst stimulation (Titiz et al., 2017), have also been shown to optimally induce long-term potentiation (LTP) (Larson and Munkácsy, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited studies.

claim: Theta phase reset occurs in response to novel sensory input or electrical stimulation applied to the fornix or perforant path.
source: Another potential mechanism underlying the effect of hippocampal neurostimulation might be the reset of the phase of theta oscillations in response to exogenous inputs, such as a novel sensory input or a pulse of electrical stimulation applied to the fornix or perforant path (Buño et al., 1978; Williams and Givens, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: Theta phase reset facilitates long-term potentiation.
source: Theta phase reset is known to facilitate LTP (McCartney et al., 2004) and naturally occurs during both encoding and retrieval of associative memories (Kota et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited studies.

claim: Theta phase reset naturally occurs during both encoding and retrieval of associative memories.
source: Theta phase reset is known to facilitate LTP (McCartney et al., 2004) and naturally occurs during both encoding and retrieval of associative memories (Kota et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: Models of memory-related theta-gamma oscillations in the hippocampal formation have been developed across different resolution levels.
source: Models of memory-related theta-gamma oscillations in the hippocampal formation have been developed across different resolution levels, ranging from abstract mean-field approaches (Traub et al., 1997; Onslow et al., 2014; Segneri et al., 2020) to biophysically realistic conductance-based models (Lundqvist et al., 2006; Herman et al., 2013; Aussel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling studies.

claim: Neural masses can generate gamma oscillations through reciprocal interactions between an excitatory and inhibitory population.
source: Neural masses, which represent the mean activity of a neuronal population, can generate gamma oscillations through reciprocal interactions between an excitatory and inhibitory population (Traub et al., 1997; Onslow et al., 2014), or even using a self-projecting inhibitory population (Segneri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling studies.

claim: Neural masses can generate gamma oscillations using a self-projecting inhibitory population.
source: Neural masses, which represent the mean activity of a neuronal population, can generate gamma oscillations through reciprocal interactions between an excitatory and inhibitory population (Traub et al., 1997; Onslow et al., 2014), or even using a self-projecting inhibitory population (Segneri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling study.

claim: Under excitatory oscillatory input at theta frequencies, neural mass models are capable of generating theta-nested gamma oscillations.
source: Under excitatory oscillatory input at theta frequencies, these models are capable of generating theta-nested gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is a general property of neural mass models as described in the cited literature.

claim: Theta-nested gamma oscillations can be observed in models of the hippocampal formation composed of single-compartment Hodgkin-Huxley neurons driven by a fixed oscillatory theta input.
source: Similarly, these oscillations can be observed in more complex models of the hippocampal formation composed of single-compartment excitatory and inhibitory neurons connected through conductance-based synapses following the Hodgkin-Huxley formalism (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952), and driven by a fixed oscillatory theta input (Aussel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling study.

claim: Most computational work on neurostimulation has focused on mechanisms underlying DBS of the basal ganglia for motor disorders such as Parkinson's disease.
source: In terms of neurostimulation, most computational work has focused on the mechanisms underlying DBS of the basal ganglia for motor disorders such as Parkinson's disease (Rubin and Terman, 2004; Pirini et al., 2009; Mina et al., 2013; Ebert et al., 2014), peripheral nerve stimulation (Rattay et al., 2003; Kipping and Nogueira, 2022), spinal cord stimulation (Rattay et al., 2000; Capogrosso et al., 2013), or has remained generic (Basu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling studies.

claim: Models investigating neurostimulation of hippocampal circuits are scarce and do not take into account the effects on theta-gamma oscillations.
source: However, models investigating neurostimulation of hippocampal circuits are scarce (Hendrickson et al., 2016; Bingham et al., 2018) and do not take into account the effects on theta-gamma oscillations.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the literature based on the authors' review.

claim: A detailed multicompartment model of the rat dentate gyrus was able to replicate experimentally recorded local field potentials induced by different electrode placements and pulse amplitudes during stimulation of the perforant path.
source: For example, a detailed multicompartment model of the rat dentate gyrus was able to replicate experimentally recorded local field potentials induced by different electrode placements and pulse amplitudes during stimulation of the perforant path (Bingham et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling study.

claim: Kuramoto phase oscillators have been used to model the impact of neurostimulation on neuronal oscillations in the context of Parkinson's disease and essential tremor.
source: To model the impact of neurostimulation on neuronal oscillations, a more abstract formalism based on Kuramoto phase oscillators (Kuramoto, 1984) has been introduced in the context of Parkinson's disease and essential tremor, which enabled the design of novel neurostimulation paradigms that enhance or disrupt neuronal synchrony in basal ganglia circuits (Tass, 2003; Ebert et al., 2014; Asllani et al., 2018; Weerasinghe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling studies.

claim: There is currently no model of the hippocampal formation that is able to replicate both theta-gamma PAC and theta phase reset during neurostimulation.
source: To our knowledge, there is currently no model of the hippocampal formation that is able to replicate both theta-gamma PAC and theta phase reset during neurostimulation.
evidence: This is a knowledge gap identified by the authors based on their literature review.

claim: The authors modified an existing biophysical model of the hippocampal formation by Aussel et al., 2018.
source: To investigate the effects of neurostimulation on hippocampal circuits while taking into account these two mechanisms, we modified an existing biophysical model of the hippocampal formation (Aussel et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the methodological approach taken in the study.

claim: In the original model by Aussel et al., the theta rhythm was considered as an oscillatory input of fixed amplitude and phase velocity, which is inconsistent with theta phase reset.
source: In this original model, however, the theta rhythm was considered as an oscillatory input of fixed amplitude and phase velocity, which is inconsistent with theta phase reset.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of the previous model.

claim: The authors combined the biophysical model with abstract Kuramoto oscillators that acted as a dynamical source of theta rhythm, modeling medial septum inputs to the hippocampal formation.
source: To circumvent this limitation, we combined this biophysical model with abstract Kuramoto oscillators that acted as a dynamical source of theta rhythm, thereby modeling medial septum inputs to the hippocampal formation.
evidence: This describes the key methodological innovation of the study.

claim: The new hybrid dynamical model could generate both theta-nested gamma oscillations and theta phase reset.
source: This new hybrid dynamical model could generate both theta-nested gamma oscillations and theta phase reset, following a particular phase response curve (PRC) inspired by experimental literature (Lengyel et al., 2005; Akam et al., 2012; Torben-Nielsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a key result demonstrating the capabilities of the model.

claim: The phase response curve of the model was inspired by experimental literature.
source: This new hybrid dynamical model could generate both theta-nested gamma oscillations and theta phase reset, following a particular phase response curve (PRC) inspired by experimental literature (Lengyel et al., 2005; Akam et al., 2012; Torben-Nielsen et al., 2010).
evidence: This indicates that the model was designed to match experimental observations.

claim: In the absence of theta input from the medial septum, single-pulse stimulation produced a transient effect consisting of one or several bursts of activity, depending on stimulation amplitude.
source: In the absence of theta input from the medial septum, single-pulse stimulation produced a transient effect consisting of one or several bursts of activity, depending on stimulation amplitude.
evidence: This is a result from the simulations.

claim: The presence of multiple bursts in response to single-pulse stimulation depended on the single-cell calcium dynamics and M-type potassium adaptation current.
source: The presence of multiple bursts depended on the single-cell calcium dynamics and M-type potassium adaptation current.
evidence: This is a mechanistic finding from the simulations.

claim: In the presence of weak theta input, single-pulse stimulation could produce long-lasting or even persistent activity by switching the network to a highly synchronized state characterized by theta-nested gamma oscillations.
source: In the presence of weak theta input, designed to mimic a pathological state that impairs theta-gamma oscillations, single-pulse stimulation could produce long-lasting or even persistent activity by switching the network to a highly synchronized state characterized by theta-nested gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is a key result from the simulations.

claim: When phase reset was not included in the model, the effect of single-pulse stimulation was more pronounced when the stimulation pulse was delivered at the peak of the theta rhythm.
source: When phase reset was not included in the model, this effect was more pronounced when the stimulation pulse was delivered at the peak of the theta rhythm.
evidence: This is a result showing phase-dependent effects in the absence of phase reset.

claim: When strong theta reset was considered, the phase at which stimulation was delivered did not influence the outcome.
source: However, when strong theta reset was considered, the phase at which stimulation was delivered did not influence the outcome.
evidence: This is a result showing that phase reset eliminates phase-dependent effects.

claim: In the presence of an even weaker theta input, only pulse train stimulation could restore physiological theta-gamma oscillations during the stimulation period.
source: In the presence of an even weaker theta input, mimicking a pathological state that completely abolishes theta-gamma oscillations, only pulse train stimulation could restore physiological theta-gamma oscillations during the stimulation period.
evidence: This is a result from the simulations.

claim: The effect of pulse train stimulation was phase-dependent only when theta reset was not included.
source: As for the previous results, this effect was phase-dependent only when theta reset was not included.
evidence: This is a result showing the role of phase reset in determining phase-dependent effects.

claim: A network of interconnected pyramidal neurons and interneurons can give rise to oscillations in the gamma range through a mechanism termed pyramidal-interneuronal network gamma (PING).
source: It is well established that a network of interconnected pyramidal neurons and interneurons can give rise to oscillations in the gamma range, a mechanism termed pyramidal-interneuronal network gamma (PING) (Traub et al., 2004; Onslow et al., 2014; Segneri et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited studies.

claim: PING mechanism has been observed in optogenetic studies with gradually increasing light intensity affecting multiple different circuits.
source: This mechanism has been observed in several optogenetic studies with gradually increasing light intensity (i.e. under a ramp input) affecting multiple different circuits, such as layer 2–3 pyramidal neurons of the mouse somatosensory cortex (Adesnik and Scanziani, 2010), the CA3 field of the hippocampus in rat in vitro slices (Akam et al., 2012), and in the non-human primate motor cortex (Lu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: In optogenetic studies, gamma oscillations emerged above a certain threshold in terms of photostimulation intensity.
source: In all cases, gamma oscillations emerged above a certain threshold in terms of photostimulation intensity, and the frequency of these oscillations was either stable or slightly increased when increasing the intensity further.
evidence: This is a general observation from the cited experimental studies.

claim: The model replicated the emergence of gamma oscillations above a certain input threshold, with oscillations asymptotically reaching a frequency of about 60 Hz.
source: As the amplitude of the input increased, the activity of both neuronal populations became synchronized in the gamma range, asymptotically reaching a frequency of about 60 Hz (Figure 2A bottom panel).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Decoupling the excitatory and inhibitory populations led to the abolition of gamma oscillations.
source: Decoupling the populations led to the abolition of gamma oscillations (Figure 2B), as neuronal activity was determined solely by the intrinsic properties of each cell.
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When the ramp input was provided solely to the excitatory population, the activity of the pyramidal neurons preceded the activity of the inhibitory neurons, while still preserving the emergence of gamma oscillations.
source: Interestingly, when the ramp input was provided solely to the excitatory population, we observed that the activity of the pyramidal neurons preceded the activity of the inhibitory neurons, while still preserving the emergence of gamma oscillations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the absence of noise, each population could generate by itself gamma oscillations that were purely driven by the input and determined by the intrinsic properties of the neurons.
source: Interestingly, in the absence of noise, each population could generate by itself gamma oscillations that were purely driven by the input and determined by the intrinsic properties of the neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Adding stochastic Gaussian noise in the membrane potential disrupted artificial oscillations in decoupled populations.
source: Adding stochastic Gaussian noise in the membrane potential disrupted these artificial oscillations in decoupled populations (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Pulsed optogenetic stimulation of fast-spiking inhibitory neurons at gamma frequencies can induce gamma oscillations in the neocortex and hippocampal CA1.
source: Another potent way to induce gamma oscillations is to drive fast-spiking inhibitory neurons using pulsed optogenetic stimulation at gamma frequencies, a strategy that has been used both in the neocortex (Cardin et al., 2009) and hippocampal CA1 (Iaccarino et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: Cardin and colleagues showed that fast-spiking interneurons are preferentially entrained around 40–50 Hz, while excitatory neurons respond better to lower frequencies.
source: In particular, Cardin and colleagues systematically investigated the effect of driving either excitatory or fast-spiking inhibitory neocortical neurons at frequencies between 10 and 200 Hz (Cardin et al., 2009). They showed that fast-spiking interneurons are preferentially entrained around 40–50 Hz, while excitatory neurons respond better to lower frequencies.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental study.

claim: The model replicated the finding that interneurons showed the greatest degree of gamma power modulation when presented with continuous stimulation across a range of frequencies in the gamma range.
source: When presented with continuous stimulation across a range of frequencies in the gamma range, interneurons showed the greatest degree of gamma power modulation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: When stimulation was delivered to the excitatory population, the relative power around the stimulation frequency dropped significantly in frequencies above 10 Hz.
source: Furthermore, when the stimulation was delivered to the excitatory population, the relative power around the stimulation frequency dropped significantly in frequencies above 10 Hz, similar to the reported experimental data (Cardin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations that matches experimental data.

claim: The input theta rhythm drove the network to produce spiking activity in the gamma range preferentially around the peak of theta in all excitatory and inhibitory populations.
source: As in the original model (Aussel et al., 2018), the input theta rhythm drove the network to produce spiking activity in the gamma range preferentially around the peak of theta in all excitatory and inhibitory populations (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Spectrograms of the CA1 population firing rates revealed that bursts of activity around each theta peak were characterized by oscillations around 60 Hz.
source: Spectrograms of the CA1 population firing rates revealed that these bursts of activity around each theta peak were characterized by oscillations around 60 Hz (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Power spectral densities showed a clear peak at 4 Hz (corresponding to the theta drive) and increases in gamma band activity between 40 and 80 Hz.
source: This was confirmed by power spectral densities, which showed a clear peak at 4 Hz (corresponding to the theta drive) and increases in gamma band activity between 40 and 80 Hz (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The modulation index (MI) has been shown to outperform other similar measures for quantifying PAC.
source: To quantify PAC between theta and gamma oscillations, we used the modulation index (MI) (Tort et al., 2008; Tort et al., 2010), which has been shown to outperform other similar measures (Hülsemann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: The MI metric would give erroneous results in simulated datasets due to the absence of certain frequency components.
source: However, we discovered that this metric would give erroneous results in our simulated datasets due to the absence of certain frequency components.
evidence: This is an observation made by the authors during their analysis.

claim: Uniform noise was added to the firing rates prior to computing the MI to overcome limitations and avoid artifacts.
source: To overcome this limitation and avoid artifacts, uniform noise was added to the firing rates prior to computing the MI (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a methodological choice made by the authors.

claim: Analysis confirmed that gamma-band signals between 45 and 75 Hz were modulated by lower theta frequencies between 3 and 6 Hz.
source: This analysis confirmed that gamma-band signals between 45 and 75 Hz were modulated by lower theta frequencies between 3 and 6 Hz, which we quantified by computing a global MI in frequency ranges encompassing theta (3–9 Hz) and gamma (40–80 Hz) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Oscillations between 40 and 80 Hz occur preferentially around the peak of theta.
source: To refine this analysis, we also computed a similar MI between the amplitude of various gamma frequencies and the phase of theta, which indicated that oscillations between 40 and 80 Hz occur preferentially around the peak of theta (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The model was able to display theta phase reset during single-pulse stimulation.
source: Next, we verified that our model was able to display theta phase reset during single-pulse stimulation (depolarizing pulse, 1 ms duration).
evidence: This is a result demonstrating a key capability of the model.

claim: PRCs of individual pyramidal cells in the CA3 and CA1 fields of the hippocampus appear biphasic and show a phase advancement for stimuli delivered in the ascending slope of theta and a delay for stimuli delivered in the descending slope.
source: Although there is no direct measurement of the PRC of septal neurons, such characterizations have been performed for individual pyramidal cells in the CA3 and CA1 fields of the hippocampus (Lengyel et al., 2005; Kwag and Paulsen, 2009; Akam et al., 2012). These PRCs appear biphasic and show a phase advancement (respectively delay) for stimuli delivered in the ascending (respectively descending) slope of theta.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: The authors modeled the biphasic PRC behavior by a specific term called the phase response function in the general equation of the Kuramoto oscillators.
source: We modeled this behavior by a specific term (which we called the phase response function) in the general equation of the Kuramoto oscillators (see methods, Equation 1).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the model design.

claim: Introducing a phase offset in the phase response function disrupted theta-nested gamma oscillations.
source: Importantly, introducing a phase offset in the phase response function disrupted theta-nested gamma oscillations (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), which suggests that the septohippocampal circuitry must be critically tuned to be able to generate such oscillations.
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The septohippocampal circuitry must be critically tuned to be able to generate theta-nested gamma oscillations.
source: Importantly, introducing a phase offset in the phase response function disrupted theta-nested gamma oscillations (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), which suggests that the septohippocampal circuitry must be critically tuned to be able to generate such oscillations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that phase offset disrupts oscillations.

claim: A single stimulation pulse delivered to all excitatory and inhibitory CA1 neurons could reset the phase of theta to a value close to its peaks.
source: In the presence of the physiological phase response function and of a sufficiently high reset gain, a single stimulation pulse delivered to all excitatory and inhibitory CA1 neurons could reset the phase of theta to a value close to its peaks (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The neuronal network behaved according to the phase response function set in the Kuramoto oscillators.
source: We computed the PRC of our simulated data for different stimulation amplitudes and validated that our neuronal network behaved according to the phase response function set in our Kuramoto oscillators (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a validation result shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Including the phase reset mechanism affected the generated theta rhythm even in the absence of stimulation, extending the duration of the theta peak and thereby slowing down the frequency of the generated theta rhythm.
source: It should be noted that including this phase reset mechanism affected the generated theta rhythm even in the absence of stimulation, extending the duration of the theta peak and thereby slowing down the frequency of the generated theta rhythm.
evidence: This is an observation about the effect of the phase reset mechanism on the model behavior.

claim: The general approach of interfacing Kuramoto oscillators with other models is generalizable and can be applied to other models producing theta-nested gamma oscillations.
source: Importantly, our approach is generalizable and can be applied to other models producing theta-nested gamma oscillations. For instance, we adapted the neural mass model by Onslow and colleagues (Onslow et al., 2014), replaced the fixed theta input by a set of Kuramoto oscillators, and demonstrated that it could also generate theta phase reset in response to single-pulse stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The general behavior of the model is not specific to the tuning of individual parameters in the conductance-based neurons, but follows general rules that are captured by the level of abstraction of the Kuramoto formalism.
source: These results illustrate that the general behavior of our model is not specific to the tuning of individual parameters in the conductance-based neurons, but follows general rules that are captured by the level of abstraction of the Kuramoto formalism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the generalizability demonstrated with the neural mass model.

claim: In the absence of theta drive, a single stimulation pulse elicited either zero or two bursts of spiking activity depending on stimulation amplitude, separated by about 200 ms.
source: In the absence of theta drive, a single stimulation pulse elicited either zero or two bursts of spiking activity (depending on stimulation amplitude) separated by about 200 ms (Figure 4A and C).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 4A and C.

claim: A previous model has shown that the presence of Calcium-Activated Non-specific cationic (CAN) currents can lead to self-sustained theta oscillations in the hippocampus.
source: A previous model has shown that the presence of Calcium-Activated Non-specific cationic (CAN) currents can lead to self-sustained theta oscillations in the hippocampus (Giovannini et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling study.

claim: The CAN current is directly linked to the spike-frequency adaptation properties of the M current, affecting transitions from an asynchronous low-firing regime to synchronous bursting.
source: Moreover, this study showed a direct link between the increased excitation provided by the CAN current and the spike-frequency adaptation properties of the M current, directly affecting transitions from an asynchronous low-firing regime to synchronous bursting.
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling study.

claim: Completely removing the CAN current from the simulations abolished the second burst of activity in response to single-pulse stimulation.
source: We tested the role of the CAN current in the response to single-pulse stimulation by completely removing it from our simulations, which abolished the second burst of activity (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The time interval separating the two bursts likely resulted from the interplay between the depolarizing CAN current and hyperpolarizing M current.
source: Moreover, the time interval separating the two bursts likely resulted from the interplay between the depolarizing CAN current and hyperpolarizing M current (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: In the presence of dynamic theta input, the effects of single-pulse stimulation depended both on theta input amplitude and stimulation amplitude, highlighting different regimes of network activity.
source: In the presence of dynamic theta input, the effects of single-pulse stimulation depended both on theta input amplitude and stimulation amplitude, highlighting different regimes of network activity (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 5 and supplements.

claim: For low theta input, theta-nested gamma oscillations were initially absent and could not be induced by stimulation.
source: For low theta input, theta-nested gamma oscillations were initially absent and could not be induced by stimulation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For increasing theta input, the network switched to an intermediate regime where a single stimulation pulse of sufficiently high amplitude could kick it to a state with self-sustained theta-nested gamma oscillations.
source: For increasing theta input, the network switched to an intermediate regime: upon initialization at a state with no spiking activity, it could be kicked to a state with self-sustained theta-nested gamma oscillations by a single stimulation pulse of sufficiently high amplitude (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The intermediate regime existed for a range of septal theta inputs located just below the threshold to induce self-sustained theta-gamma oscillations without additional stimulation.
source: This regime existed for a range of septal theta inputs located just below the threshold to induce self-sustained theta-gamma oscillations without additional stimulation, as characterized by the post-stimulation theta power, gamma power, and theta-gamma PAC (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Removing CAN currents from all areas of the model abolished the ability of single-pulse stimulation to induce self-sustained theta-nested gamma oscillations.
source: Removing CAN currents from all areas of the model abolished this behavior (Figure 5 - figure supplement 4), which is interesting given the role of this current in the multistability of EC neurons (Egorov et al., 2002; Fransén et al., 2006) and in the intrinsic ability of the hippocampus to generate theta-nested gamma oscillations (Giovannini et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 5 - figure supplement 4.

claim: The CAN current plays a role in the multistability of EC neurons.
source: Removing CAN currents from all areas of the model abolished this behavior (Figure 5 - figure supplement 4), which is interesting given the role of this current in the multistability of EC neurons (Egorov et al., 2002; Fransén et al., 2006) and in the intrinsic ability of the hippocampus to generate theta-nested gamma oscillations (Giovannini et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited studies.

claim: The CAN current plays a role in the intrinsic ability of the hippocampus to generate theta-nested gamma oscillations.
source: Removing CAN currents from all areas of the model abolished this behavior (Figure 5 - figure supplement 4), which is interesting given the role of this current in the multistability of EC neurons (Egorov et al., 2002; Fransén et al., 2006) and in the intrinsic ability of the hippocampus to generate theta-nested gamma oscillations (Giovannini et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited study.

claim: For the highest theta input, the network became able to spontaneously generate theta-nested gamma oscillations, even when initialized at a state with no spiking activity and without additional neurostimulation.
source: For the highest theta input, the network became able to spontaneously generate theta-nested gamma oscillations, even when initialized at a state with no spiking activity and without additional neurostimulation Figure 5C.
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the case of a moderate theta input and in the presence of phase reset, delivering a pulse at either the peak or trough of theta could induce theta-nested gamma oscillations.
source: In the case of a moderate theta input and in the presence of phase reset, delivering a pulse at either the peak or trough of theta could induce theta-nested gamma oscillations (Figure 6A and C).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 6A and C.

claim: In the absence of phase reset, only stimulation delivered at the peak of theta was able to induce theta-nested gamma oscillations.
source: By contrast, in the absence of phase reset, only stimulation delivered at the peak of theta was able to induce such oscillations, after some time delay (Figure 6B and D).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: With phase reset, pulse train stimulation restored theta-nested gamma oscillations within the whole network, irrespective of the phase of stimulation onset.
source: With phase reset, pulse train stimulation restored theta-nested gamma oscillations within the whole network, irrespective of the phase of stimulation onset (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 7A and C.

claim: Stimulation delivered at the trough forced a reset of the phase of theta rhythm and led to the subsequent delivery of pulses at the peak of theta.
source: Notably, stimulation delivered at the trough forced a reset of the phase of theta rhythm and led to the subsequent delivery of pulses at the peak of theta.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations.

claim: In the absence of phase reset, peak-targeted stimulation induced theta-gamma oscillations in all network areas easily, while trough-targeted stimulation created artificial bursts that propagated in other areas with difficulty.
source: Interestingly, in the absence of phase reset, peak-targeted stimulation induced theta-gamma oscillations in all network areas easily, while trough-targeted stimulation created artificial bursts that propagated in other areas with difficulty, requiring multiple pulses to achieve a fraction of the results of peak-targeted stimulation (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 7B and D.

claim: The key innovation compared to previous models is the introduction of a set of abstract Kuramoto oscillators representing pacemaker neurons in the medial septum interfaced with biophysically realistic neuronal models in the hippocampus.
source: The key innovation compared to previous models (e.g. Aussel et al., 2018) is the introduction of a set of abstract Kuramoto oscillators, which represent pacemaker neurons in the medial septum and are interfaced with biophysically realistic neuronal models in the hippocampus.
evidence: This summarizes the main methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The hybrid interfacing between two levels of abstraction represents a methodological innovation that could be applied to other systems or brain structures driven by dynamical rhythms.
source: From a methodological point of view, this hybrid interfacing between two levels of abstraction represents an innovation in itself and could be applied to other systems or brain structures that are driven by dynamical rhythms.
evidence: This is a claim about the broader applicability of the methodological approach.

claim: Delivering a single stimulation pulse bilaterally to the human hippocampus during a memory task is sufficient to impair memory encoding.
source: Nevertheless, delivering a single stimulation pulse bilaterally to the human hippocampus during a memory task is sufficient to impair memory encoding (Lacruz et al., 2010), suggesting that even single-pulse stimulation can indeed have wide network effects that are behaviorally relevant.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental study.

claim: Human intracranial stimulation data indicate that the receptivity of hippocampal circuits to single-pulse stimulation is modulated by the phase of theta.
source: Human intracranial stimulation data indicate that the receptivity of hippocampal circuits to single-pulse stimulation is modulated by the phase of theta (Lurie et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental study.

claim: Conflicting results in terms of memory outcomes could potentially be attributed to the induction of phase reset through stimulation.
source: A number of studies have also reported conflicting results in terms of memory outcomes, which could potentially be attributed to the induction of phase reset through stimulation (Suthana et al., 2012; Jacobs et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the cited studies and the model results.

claim: The degree of phase reset that follows each stimulation pulse remains unknown and should be investigated in future experimental studies.
source: To our knowledge, however, the degree of phase reset that follows each stimulation pulse remains unknown and should be investigated in future experimental studies.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap and suggests future research directions.

claim: Phase-triggered stimulation would be most useful if the phase reset mechanism remains relatively limited.
source: Such phase-triggered stimulation would be most useful if the phase reset mechanism remains relatively limited.
evidence: This is an inference based on the model results.

claim: When the phase reset mechanism becomes too strong, regular continuous stimulation appears sufficient to restore physiological theta-gamma oscillations.
source: When this mechanism becomes too strong, regular continuous stimulation appears sufficient to restore physiological theta-gamma oscillations (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an inference based on the simulation results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The degree of theta phase reset is dynamic, depending on the environment and associated task requirements.
source: In reality, the degree of theta phase reset is dynamic, depending on the environment and associated task requirements (Rizzuto et al., 2003; Mormann et al., 2005; Jackson et al., 2008), and may be affected by neurodegenerative disorders that affect the connections between the hippocampal formation and the medial septum.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: The degree of theta phase reset may be affected by neurodegenerative disorders that affect the connections between the hippocampal formation and the medial septum.
source: In reality, the degree of theta phase reset is dynamic, depending on the environment and associated task requirements (Rizzuto et al., 2003; Mormann et al., 2005; Jackson et al., 2008), and may be affected by neurodegenerative disorders that affect the connections between the hippocampal formation and the medial septum.
evidence: This is a speculation based on knowledge of neurodegenerative disorders.

claim: The proposed framework can simulate intermediate values of the reset gain, which should ideally be fitted to experimental data in future applications.
source: Importantly, our proposed framework can simulate intermediate values of the reset gain, which should ideally be fitted to experimental data in future applications.
evidence: This describes a capability of the model and suggests future work.

claim: The choice to reduce theta input amplitude was meant to simulate neurodegeneration in the medial septum, which is known to be affected in Alzheimer's disease, leading to oscillatory disruptions.
source: This choice was meant to simulate neurodegeneration in the medial septum, which is known to be affected in Alzheimer's disease, leading to oscillatory disruptions (Nelson et al., 2014; Hampel et al., 2018; Takeuchi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the cited studies on Alzheimer's disease.

claim: Reducing the synchronization parameter to simulate reduced ability of septal pacemaker neurons to synchronize had less pronounced effects on hippocampal oscillations.
source: Another possibility would be that neurodegeneration limits the ability of the septal pacemaker neurons to synchronize, thus producing a weaker collective theta rhythm without affecting the maximum amplitude of individual oscillators. Although we simulated this change in our model by reducing the synchronization parameter, the effects on hippocampal oscillations were less pronounced (Figure 5 - figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a result from the simulations shown in Figure 5 - figure supplement 5.

claim: The model deliberately modeled only a single theta generator, while multiple intra- and extra-hippocampal generators are known to co-exist.
source: In particular, we deliberately modeled only a single theta generator, while multiple intra- and extra-hippocampal generators are known to co-exist (Kocsis et al., 1999; Hummos and Nair, 2017).
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The authors decided to model septal pacemaker neurons projecting to the EC as the main source of hippocampal theta as reported in multiple experimental studies.
source: We decided to model septal pacemaker neurons projecting to the EC as the main source of hippocampal theta as reported in multiple experimental studies (Buzsáki, 2002; Buzsáki et al., 2003; Hangya et al., 2009; Colgin, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: Experimental findings and previous models have proposed that direct septal inputs are not essential for theta generation but play an important role in phase synchronization of hippocampal neurons.
source: However, experimental findings and previous models have also proposed that direct septal inputs are not essential for theta generation (Wang, 2002; Colgin, 2013; Mysin et al., 2019), but play an important role in phase synchronization of hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by the cited studies.

claim: The model does not account for the connections between the lateral and medial septum and the hippocampus.
source: Furthermore, the model does not account for the connections between the lateral and medial septum and the hippocampus (Takeuchi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: An experimental study has highlighted the importance of the lateral septum in regulating the hippocampal theta rhythm.
source: An experimental study has highlighted the importance of the lateral septum in regulating the hippocampal theta rhythm Bender et al., 2015, an area that has not been included in the model.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental study.

claim: Theta-rhythmic optogenetic stimulation of the axonal projections from the lateral septum to the hippocampus was shown to entrain theta oscillations and lead to behavioral changes during exploration in transgenic mice.
source: Specifically, theta-rhythmic optogenetic stimulation of the axonal projections from the lateral septum to the hippocampus was shown to entrain theta oscillations and lead to behavioral changes during exploration in transgenic mice.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental study (Bender et al., 2015).

claim: The model made an important simplification by considering only basket cells as the main class of inhibitory interneuron in the whole hippocampal formation.
source: In terms of neuronal cell types, we also made an important simplification by considering only basket cells as the main class of inhibitory interneuron in the whole hippocampal formation.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Many other types of interneurons exist in the hippocampus and have been modeled in various works with higher computational complexity.
source: However, it should be noted that many other types of interneurons exist in the hippocampus and have been modeled in various works with higher computational complexity (e.g. Bezaire et al., 2016; Chatzikalymniou et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling studies.

claim: Oriens-lacunosum moleculare (OLM) neurons in the CA1 field have been shown to play a crucial role in synchronizing the activity of pyramidal neurons at gamma frequencies.
source: Among these various interneurons, oriens-lacunosum moleculare (OLM) neurons in the CA1 field have been shown to play a crucial role in synchronizing the activity of pyramidal neurons at gamma frequencies (Tort et al., 2007), and in generating theta-gamma PAC (e.g. Neymotin et al., 2011; Ponzi et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by the cited studies.

claim: OLM cells may contribute to the formation of specific phase relationships within CA1 neuronal populations through the integration between inputs from the medial septum, the EC, and CA3.
source: Additionally, these cells may contribute to the formation of specific phase relationships within CA1 neuronal populations, through the integration between inputs from the medial septum, the EC, and CA3 (Mysin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling study.

claim: The model largely neglected synaptic transmission delays, which could affect the phase relationships between the medial septum and different hippocampal subfields.
source: Another limitation of our model concerns synaptic transmission delays, which have been largely neglected and could affect the phase relationships between the medial septum and different hippocampal subfields.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Experimental studies have reported time delays in the population activities of connected anatomical structures.
source: Experimental studies have indeed reported time delays in the population activities of connected anatomical structures (i.e. from EC to DG; Mizuseki et al., 2009), with pyramidal cells in downstream areas like CA3 and CA1 preferentially firing at different phases of theta (Dragoi and Buzsáki, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: The model represented only a thin coronal slice of the hippocampal formation, and it remains unclear how an anatomically accurate model of the whole structure would behave in terms of propagation of spontaneous and electrically-induced neuronal activity.
source: We also decided to represent only a thin coronal slice of the hippocampal formation, and it remains unclear how an anatomically accurate model of the whole structure would behave in terms of propagation of spontaneous and electrically-induced neuronal activity.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The model did not consider learning through synaptic plasticity, even though such mechanisms could drastically modify synaptic conduction for the whole network.
source: Importantly, we did not consider learning through synaptic plasticity, even though such mechanisms could drastically modify synaptic conduction for the whole network (Borges et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The inclusion of spike-timing-dependent plasticity would enable the investigation of stimulation protocols aimed at promoting LTP, such as theta-burst stimulation.
source: Even more interestingly, the inclusion of spike-timing-dependent plasticity would enable the investigation of stimulation protocols aimed at promoting LTP, such as theta-burst stimulation (Larson and Munkácsy, 2015).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work supported by the cited study.

claim: Future work is needed to extend the current model to a multi-compartment representation of neurites, since axons are known to be preferentially activated by extracellular electrical stimulation.
source: From the point of view of neurostimulation, future work is needed to extend the current model to a multi-compartment representation of neurites, since axons are known to be preferentially activated by extracellular electrical stimulation (Rattay et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future work supported by the cited study.

claim: Multi-compartment cable models have been developed to investigate spike initiation and propagation by modeling the axon as a series of resistance-capacitance circuits following its trajectory.
source: Specifically, multi-compartment cable models have been developed to investigate spike initiation and propagation by modeling the axon as a series of resistance-capacitance circuits following its trajectory (Rattay et al., 2003; Joucla and Yvert, 2012; Ashida and Nogueira, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling studies.

claim: The effects of extracellular stimulation are non-intuitive and depend as a first approximation on the second spatial derivative of the electrical potential along the cell membrane.
source: These models are particularly suited to study the effects of extracellular stimulation, which are non-intuitive and depend as a first approximation on the second spatial derivative of the electrical potential along the cell membrane (Rattay, 1986; Rattay et al., 2003; McIntyre et al., 2004; Rattay et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited studies.

claim: The authors modeled electrical stimulation as an intracellular current applied equally across all neurons in the targeted area, which is extremely simplified but enables computational tractability.
source: Here, we have modeled electrical stimulation as an intracellular current applied equally across all neurons in the targeted area, which is extremely simplified but enables computational tractability.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The authors likened conditions of low theta input to pathological states characteristic of oscillopathies such as Alzheimer's disease.
source: Finally, we likened conditions of low theta input to pathological states characteristic of oscillopathies such as Alzheimer's disease, as these conditions disrupted all aspects of theta-gamma oscillations in our model: theta power, gamma power, and theta-gamma PAC (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a modeling choice made by the authors.

claim: Changes in theta or gamma power in Alzheimer's disease are often unclear, and the most consistent alteration reported is a reduction of theta-gamma PAC.
source: However, it should be noted that changes in theta or gamma power in these pathologies are often unclear, and that the most consistent alteration that has been reported in Alzheimer's disease is a reduction of theta-gamma PAC (for review, see Kitchigina, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited review.

claim: GABAergic neurons from the medial septum project to the EC, CA3, and CA1 fields of the hippocampus.
source: Biologically, GABAergic neurons from the medial septum project to the EC, CA3, and CA1 fields of the hippocampus (Tóth et al., 1993; Hajós et al., 2004; Manseau et al., 2008; Hangya et al., 2009; Unal et al., 2015; Müller and Remy, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: Previous computational studies have suggested that the direct projection from the medial septum to CA1 is not essential for the production of theta in CA1 microcircuits.
source: Although the respective roles of these different projections are not fully understood, previous computational studies have suggested that the direct projection from the medial septum to CA1 is not essential for the production of theta in CA1 microcircuits (Mysin et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling study.

claim: The model used a simplified representation where the medial septum projects only to the EC, which in turn drives the different subfields of the hippocampus.
source: Since our modeling of the medial septum is only used to generate a dynamic theta rhythm, we opted for a simplified representation where the medial septum projects only to the EC, which in turn drives the different subfields of the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a modeling choice made by the authors.

claim: The model is composed of excitatory-inhibitory (E-I) circuits connected in series, with a feedback loop going through a population of coupled phase oscillators.
source: From a conceptual point of view, our model is thus composed of excitatory-inhibitory (E-I) circuits connected in series, with a feedback loop going through a population of coupled phase oscillators.
evidence: This describes the conceptual structure of the model.

claim: The model contained excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations in the entorhinal cortex (EC), dentate gyrus (DG), CA3 and CA1 fields within a coronal slice of the human hippocampus.
source: The hippocampal model contained excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations in the entorhinal cortex (EC), dentate gyrus (DG), CA3 and CA1 fields within a coronal slice of the human hippocampus (Figure 1B–C).
evidence: This describes the structure of the hippocampal model.

claim: The output of the hippocampal formation (i.e. the activity of CA1 pyramidal neurons) was provided as an input to the Kuramoto oscillators, simulating the hippocampal-septal projections through the fornix.
source: The output of the hippocampal formation (i.e. the activity of CA1 pyramidal neurons) was provided as an input to the Kuramoto oscillators, simulating the hippocampal-septal projections through the fornix (Williams and Givens, 2003; Nuñez and Buño, 2021; Takeuchi et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the feedback connection in the model, supported by the cited studies.

claim: The oscillations produced by the collective behavior of Kuramoto oscillators represented a population average of their activity: highly synchronized and desynchronized states generated respectively high and low amplitude theta oscillations.
source: The oscillations produced by the collective behavior of Kuramoto oscillators represented a population average of their activity: highly synchronized and desynchronized states generated respectively high and low amplitude theta oscillations (Figure 1D).
evidence: This describes the behavior of the Kuramoto oscillators in the model.

claim: The number of oscillators was chosen so that their synchronization level and their frequency distribution were sufficiently close to their asymptotic behavior for a large number of oscillators.
source: The number of oscillators was chosen so that their synchronization level (i.e. their order parameter) and their frequency distribution were sufficiently close to their asymptotic behavior for a large number of oscillators (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes a methodological choice in the model design.

claim: The medial septum contains pacemaker neurons that synchronize with one another and generate a global theta rhythm.
source: The medial septum contains pacemaker neurons (Varga et al., 2008; Hangya et al., 2009) that synchronize with one another and generate a global theta rhythm.
evidence: This is supported by the cited experimental studies.

claim: Kuramoto oscillators have been used to investigate the effects of neurostimulation on synchronized brain rhythms in the context of Parkinson's disease or essential tremor.
source: Kuramoto oscillators have also been used to investigate the effects of neurostimulation on synchronized brain rhythms in the context of Parkinson's disease or essential tremor (Tass, 2003; Weerasinghe et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited modeling studies.

claim: Neurons were modeled as conductance-based single compartments, following the Hodgkin-Huxley formalism.
source: Neurons were modeled as conductance-based single compartments, following the Hodgkin-Huxley formalism (Hodgkin and Huxley, 1952), in line with previous work (Aussel et al., 2022; Aussel et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the neuronal modeling approach.

claim: Excitatory neurons represent pyramidal cells in EC, CA3, and CA1, and granule cells in DG.
source: Excitatory neurons represent pyramidal cells in EC, CA3, and CA1, and granule cells in DG.
evidence: This describes the cell types represented in the model.

claim: The ratio between pyramidal neurons and interneurons was kept as a ratio of 10:1 for all areas except the dentate gyrus, where the ratio was 100:1.
source: The ratio between pyramidal neurons and interneurons was kept as a ratio of 10:1 for all areas except the dentate gyrus, where the ratio was 100:1.
evidence: This describes the population ratios used in the model.

claim: The model was implemented with the Brian2 libraries for Python.
source: The model was implemented with the Brian2 libraries for Python (Stimberg et al., 2019; see Data availability section for access to the code).
evidence: This describes the implementation of the model.

claim: Simulations were performed using a timestep of 0.1ms and a total simulation duration ranging between 3 and 10 s.
source: Simulations were performed using a timestep of 0.1ms and a total simulation duration ranging between 3 and 10 s (depending on the experiment, see results section).
evidence: This describes the simulation parameters.

claim: The average time for simulating 1 s for the complete model locally was 10 min.
source: The average time for simulating 1 s for the complete model locally was 10 min.
evidence: This describes the computational cost of the simulations.
